messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

We have an exciting, fully funded PhD opportunity in "Dynamic 
Inferential Network Analysis for Public Health" at the University of 
Glasgow. Details below. Please contact me for further information.

*Application deadline*: 12 noon, 13 January 2017

*Topic*: Dynamic Inferential Network Analysis for Public Health

*Supervisors*:
- Philip Leifeld (social sciences)
- Mark McCann (public health)
- Nema Dean (maths & stats)

*Type of funding*: This is one of the prestigious Lord Kelvin Adam Smith 
Scholarships at the University of Glasgow. Each year, a handful of 
selected PhD scholarships are granted to the best applicants. These LKAS 
scholarships are fully funded, which means that the funding includes all 
tuition fees, a stipend at RCUK rates (currently ?14,510 per year for 
2017/18), and an annual research support budget of ?3,000.

*Project summary*: The PhD candidate will work on the development and 
implementation of statistical techniques for inference on longitudinal 
networks and apply these techniques to datasets from the field of public 
health. Many public health outcomes, such as mental health or substance 
abuse, are network phenomena because they do not develop in isolation. 
It is vital for public health to understand not just the prevalence, but 
more importantly, also the causes of these "networked" health outcomes. 
Research has suggested that people's health risk behaviour and outcomes 
(e.g., smoking and obesity) may spread through networks ("contagion"); 
or may provoke network or friendship ties among people with similar 
behaviour ("homophily"). In recent years, research in network science, 
public health, the social sciences, and statistics has therefore 
developed inferential network analysis techniques for modelling the 
structure and dynamics of friendship or contact networks (e.g., the 
Temporal Exponential Random Graph Model; TERGM) and the diffusion of 
behaviour through networks over time (e.g., the Temporal Network 
Autocorrelation Model; TNAM). The innovative aspect of this project is 
the extension of the TERGM and the TNAM model to networks with multiple 
groups, multiple relations, and/or in a co-evolutionary joint process. 
This is of particular importance in public health, where behaviour like 
smoking and mental health can otherwise not be explained properly.

*Project team*: The PhD student will have the opportunity to make use of 
a variety of datasets in public health and work in an exciting 
interdisciplinary environment. The candidate will work with supervisors 
from social science research methods, public health, and statistics, 
whose joint interest is the study of network dynamics. Dr Philip Leifeld 
is a Senior Lecturer in Research Methods in the School of Social and 
Political Sciences. His research focuses on network dynamics and 
applications in the social and political sciences. Dr Mark McCann is a 
Research Fellow in the Social and Public Health Sciences Unit and is an 
expert in substance use, mental health, adolescent health behaviour, and 
complex systems. Dr Nema Dean is a Lecturer in the School of Mathematics 
and Statistics. Her research focuses on model-based inference for 
dependent and high-dimensional data. The PhD project will be hosted by 
the Graduate School of Social Sciences, and a stronger involvement in 
any of the three disciplinary homes and institutions of the supervisors 
is possible, depending on the interests of the candidate. The PhD 
project will also offer the option of a research stay abroad in the 
wider network of the three supervisors.

*Person specification*: This studentship is open to candidates of any 
nationality -- UK, EU or International. Applicants should demonstrate 
the following:

- Necessary: A strong master's degree or very strong bachelor's degree 
in one of the relevant disciplines, including any of the social 
sciences, public health, statistics, computer science, network science, 
or related disciplines.
- Desired: An interest in, or experiences with, the analysis of 
networks; an interest in public health and behaviour; a strong 
background or interest in quantitative methods and statistics; 
experiences in at least one programming language, such as R or C++.
- The ideal candidate enjoys interdisciplinary work and is intrinsically 
motivated to learn new statistical techniques and programming languages.

*Application process*: In the first instance, prospective applicants 
should contact any of the three supervisors to discuss your eligibility 
(philip.leifeld@glasgow.ac.uk; mark.mccann@glasgow.ac.uk; 
nema.dean@glasgow.ac.uk). Applicants may submit applications up until 
the application deadline of 12 noon, Friday 13 January 2017.

More details on the application procedure are available on the website 
of the Lord Kelvin Adam Smith PhD Scholarship at the University of 
Glasgow: 
http://www.gla.ac.uk/services/postgraduateresearch/scholarships/kelvinsmith/

Other PhD opportunities with me in Glasgow are available on request. 
Please distribute widely. Many thanks,

Philip

--

messages.body_plain:
Hello again,

We have yet to resolve our model convergence issue with the GWDSP term, and
were hoping to pique people?s interest in our plight.

For further background, the two networks we are running the ERGMs on are
visualized here <http://tuvalu.santafe.edu/~epower/SocialNetworks.pdf>. It
is the ?b? village that has been causing issues for us (the ?a? village
converges with GWDSP and shows model improvement over an ERGM with only
GWESP).

All our troubleshooting suggests that the issue is with GWDSP, regardless
of the other terms in the model (throwing out the other model terms doesn?t
resolve the issue, and removing GWDSP leads to model convergence). It may
have something to do with the combination of this term and the
peculiarities of this network, with its distinct clusters. As you can see
from the visualization, there are two hamlets in Village ?b? that we
thought might be effecting the GWDSP term. We tried to account for that
with particular terms for those hamlets as well as with caste nodemix terms
for the two castes to represent their segregation. Neither worked.

We also tried a few more basic troubleshooting techniques. We tried
extending the number of runs beyond 20. Similarly, we tried using the model
coefficients from a converged model without GWDSP as the starting point for
the model with GWDSP. Neither worked. We briefly tried BERGMs, but the
model diagnostics did not improve.

Any explanation as to why the GWDSP term might be causing this
non-convergence, and any suggestions as for how we might deal with it,
would be most appreciated!

- Elly & Elspeth

> Hi statnet,
>
> We?re looking for some guidance on ERGM structural control terms.
>
> Some background: We are analyzing social support networks from two
> villages, so are essentially running the same ERGM on two networks. We

> plots and seeing room for improvement. For one of the villages, adding
> GWDSP to the model (along with mutual and GWESP) improved GOF and model fit
> (AIC, BIC, etc). For the second village, adding GWDSP resulted a model that
> doesn?t converge.
>
> We?ve tried a number of things to deal with this: increasing the MCMC
> sample size and burn-in, adding more iterations (beyond the default 20),
> trying other structural control terms (gwodegree, gwidegree), as well as
> sweeping through different alpha values for the GW terms (both for all GW
> terms and just for the GWDSP term), and we tried removing other covariates
> in the model.
>
> None of this has worked. We?d like to have the two ERGMs for the two
> villages be easily comparable, ideally by including the same terms in the
> two models. Given the model improvement with GWDSP in the first village
> (and the fact that the inclusion of GWDSP alters the effect size of some

>
> 1. Does anyone have an idea of how to make GWDSP work in the model that

>

>
> 3. How should we interpret the effect of GWDSP on the first village? The

> General descriptions of the networks: ~400 nodes, ~3500 edges, directed,

>
> ERGM terms include: age, gender, a kinship network as an edgecov term, a

>
> We?ve been using both R version 3.2.3 and 3.3.0, and ergm versions 3.5.1

> Generally, we are studying the relationship between reputational standing

>
> Any help would be much, much appreciated!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Elly,

I just have time for a brief response here, and you have a lengthy set of 
questions :).

1. Note that you're using the undirected versions of these gw terms for a 
directed graph.  These only count one type of directed configuration: 
two-paths of the form A->B->C for DSP, and transitive triples of that form 
with A->C for ESP.

So, is this what you want theoretically?  If so, what does this specific 
configuration represent for your network that is of theoretical interest?

There are directed versions of the gw terms, they have the same name, with 
a "d" in front (like dgwesp).

2. Have you looked at the DSP and ESP distributions for your two datasets? 
You can do with with: summary(nw ~ esp(0:10) + dsp(0:10)).  For the gw 
versions of these terms, you want to see a smooth unimodal distribution, 
and a range that is not too constricted.  If 90+% of the frequency is 
heaped at 0 that will suggest there's too little info for the estimation 
to work with.

3. Have you tried removing the kinship network edgecov?  And is it 
directed or undirected?

It's difficult to troubleshoot a complex model like this, as both the 
univariate distributions of the statistics and the correlations among all 
of the different terms in the model are at work.

Hi, Elly -


Some general remarks first, and some specific comments on your model below -

As a general matter, the problem you are describing often arises when 
you have heterogeneous clustering (e.g., as arises from propinquity, 
homophily, shared memberships, etc.) and attempt to model it by adding a 
homogeneous term that enhances triangulation (triangles, GWESP, etc.).  
Essentially, the model can become caught between a regime in which it 
cannot add enough clustering to account for the highly clustered regions 
of the data, and a regime in which it adds too much (leading to 
convergence problems, among other things) - this is because the ideal 
model would add a lot of clustering, but only to certain parts of the graph!

The most straightforward and efficacious method for dealing with this 
problem is to identify a covariate (or function thereof) that can at 
least approximate the structure within the data, and to incorporate it 
appropriately (e.g., via nodemix, edgecov, absdiff, etc.).  In some 
cases, it may take some careful thought about the nature of the social 
process that generated the network to determine which covariates are 
needed, and how they should be used.  (As in any other model, 
transformations of the original variables are sometimes necessary.)

In some cases, a second approach related to the first is to use observed 
covariates to limit the dependence among edge variables. Right now, we 
don't have a lot of options implemented (though one could implement 
one's own terms), but the local triangle term does provide one 
alternative.  This is only likely to prove useful where each edge 
variable is exposed to relatively few potential triangles, but it may be 
worth a try in conjunction with more typical covariate effects if it is 
plausible that you are getting isolated instances of excess 
triangulation due to relationships that are selectively dependent on one 
another.

A third approach is to segment the dependence structure within the 
graph, modeling the network as blocks of ERGMs with dependence terms 
that are joined by edgewise independent ERGMs.  This is implemented in 
the hergm package, and may be worth a look.

In terms of specifics -

For the village that is not converging, your GOF plot suggests that just 
adding esp(0) might be adequate - everything else looks quite good.  For 
the one that _is_ converging, the non-GWDSP plot suggests the same 
thing.  Also, I note that you are already fitting the DSP distribution 
quite well without GWDSP in the model, so adding GWDSP would not be 
expected to improve anything.  (Recall that by adding a term to the 
model, you are restricting the expected value of the associated 
statistic to be equal to the observed value.  If this is already the 
case, one usually does not need to add an associated term, unless e.g. 
one is doing it to balance out another effect that is being added.)  
Overall, these models seem to be doing a reasonable job of recovering 
many aspects of the data, with the main and clear exception of the 
ESP0s.  (I.e., the models predict that there will be more edges not 
embedded in a triangle than there really are.)  If adding esp(0) does 
not work, my next go-to would be the kinship covariate; I don't know the 
details of your network, but in many cases embeddedness in kinship 
structures is a powerful structural influence on relationships.  You may 
need to be more creative about how you use this covariate in your 
model.  For instance, do only direct kinship ties matter?  What about 
distance in the kinship network?  What about dyads that have a kinship 
two-path?  It is possible that the enhanced ESPs you are seeing arise 
from closure that is sustained by a "backbone" of kinship ties, and a 
simple direct effect of kinship may not be adequate to capture this effect.

Hope that helps!

-Carter

Hi, Uri,

Story, then questions, then reproducible example:
I have friendship data from multiple school classes that I want to analyze with a single model, to examine homophily estimates across several different contexts. I do this by defining all my data as a single network, and specifying models with a constraint on blockdiag referring to a node-level attribute which contains the class unique id. So every model I ran on this data is specified with ?,constraints=~blockdiag('classid'). This should, according to the documentation, estimate a single model for the big table of  data, which assumes only ties between nodes with identical classid are allowed,
right?

Right.

Following several months of frustration I think I have found that either the restriction doesn't work properly or it's not working properly on the goodness of fit function. Because while my data has very few isolates, gof returns funny geodesic distance estimates, with a huge amount of paths at infinity distance, and a handful with real values. This means the restriction isn't working and any isolate is considered an isolate not only from their few class members, but from everyone, right?
For example,

#Take two networks lumped together, the first has 2 nodes, one tie, so one node with no incoming ties. The second has 3 nodes which are almost fully connected (one tie missing)

g<-matrix(0,5,5)
g[1,2]<-1
g[3,4]<-1
g[3,5]<-1
g[4,3]<-1
g[4,5]<-1
g[5,3]<-1
g<-network(g)

set.vertex.attribute(g,'class',c(1,1,2,2,2))
#With these two networks distinguishable by the attribute "class", I estimate a simple ergm model
eg<-ergm(g~edges+mutual+gwesp(0.5),contraints=~blockdiag('class'))
geg<-gof(eg,contraints=~blockdiag('class'))
geg

result - I get 13 paths of infininty length where only one such path should be present, as only the path between node 2 and node 1 is legal and of infinite length. All other infinite paths shouldn't be counted because of the constraint, no?

Indeed. gof() isn't aware of structural zeroes, except to the extent that it preserves the constraints.

 Goodness-of-fit for minimum geodesic distance

    obs min  mean max MC p-value
1     6   0  5.90  14       1.00
2     1   0  2.57  10       0.84
3     0   0  0.43   3       1.00
4     0   0  0.04   1       1.00
Inf  13   0 11.06  20       0.92

The good news is that it still produces sensible results in terms of quantiles.

 And on a related note, how can I combine several constraints? When I try

Result<-ergm(g~mutual+gwesp(0.5),constraints=~edges+blockdiag("classid"))

I get

Error in MHproposal.formula(constraints, weights = control$MCMC.prop.weights,  :

  The combination of class (c), model constraints (blockdiag+edges), reference measure (Bernoulli), and proposal weighting (default) is not implemented. Check your arguments for typos.

Unfortunately, the current framework requires a separate proposal to be implemented for every combination of constraints (with some exceptions), and a proposal that enforces both edge count and block diagonal constraints hasn't been implemented, since there hasn't been demand. This may change in the future.

I hope this helps,
Pavel

Thanks in advance for any clues as to what is going on here!
Cheers,
Uri

> Some general remarks first, and some specific comments on your model below

>
> As a general matter, the problem you are describing often arises when you
> have heterogeneous clustering (e.g., as arises from propinquity, homophily,
> shared memberships, etc.) and attempt to model it by adding a homogeneous
> term that enhances triangulation (triangles, GWESP, etc.).  Essentially,
> the model can become caught between a regime in which it cannot add enough
> clustering to account for the highly clustered regions of the data, and a
> regime in which it adds too much (leading to convergence problems, among
> other things) - this is because the ideal model would add a lot of
> clustering, but only to certain parts of the graph!
>
> The most straightforward and efficacious method for dealing with this
> problem is to identify a covariate (or function thereof) that can at least
> approximate the structure within the data, and to incorporate it
> appropriately (e.g., via nodemix, edgecov, absdiff, etc.).  In some cases,
> it may take some careful thought about the nature of the social process
> that generated the network to determine which covariates are needed, and
> how they should be used.  (As in any other model, transformations of the
> original variables are sometimes necessary.)
>
> In some cases, a second approach related to the first is to use observed
> covariates to limit the dependence among edge variables.  Right now, we
> don't have a lot of options implemented (though one could implement one's
> own terms), but the local triangle term does provide one alternative.  This
> is only likely to prove useful where each edge variable is exposed to
> relatively few potential triangles, but it may be worth a try in
> conjunction with more typical covariate effects if it is plausible that you
> are getting isolated instances of excess triangulation due to relationships
> that are selectively dependent on one another.
>
> A third approach is to segment the dependence structure within the graph,
> modeling the network as blocks of ERGMs with dependence terms that are
> joined by edgewise independent ERGMs.  This is implemented in the hergm
> package, and may be worth a look.
> In terms of specifics -
>
> For the village that is not converging, your GOF plot suggests that just
> adding esp(0) might be adequate - everything else looks quite good.  For
> the one that _is_ converging, the non-GWDSP plot suggests the same thing.
> Also, I note that you are already fitting the DSP distribution quite well
> without GWDSP in the model, so adding GWDSP would not be expected to
> improve anything.  (Recall that by adding a term to the model, you are
> restricting the expected value of the associated statistic to be equal to
> the observed value.  If this is already the case, one usually does not need
> to add an associated term, unless e.g. one is doing it to balance out
> another effect that is being added.)  Overall, these models seem to be
> doing a reasonable job of recovering many aspects of the data, with the
> main and clear exception of the ESP0s.  (I.e., the models predict that
> there will be more edges not embedded in a triangle than there really
> are.)  If adding esp(0) does not work, my next go-to would be the kinship
> covariate; I don't know the details of your network, but in many cases
> embeddedness in kinship structures is a powerful structural influence on
> relationships.  You may need to be more creative about how you use this
> covariate in your model.  For instance, do only direct kinship ties
> matter?  What about distance in the kinship network?  What about dyads that
> have a kinship two-path?  It is possible that the enhanced ESPs you are
> seeing arise from closure that is sustained by a "backbone" of kinship
> ties, and a simple direct effect of kinship may not be adequate to capture
> this effect.

> Hope that helps!

> for the clustering produced by hamlet residence/caste/kinship).
>
Martina's email certainly makes me suspect local triangles, so it might 
be worth taking a look at that again.  That's a finicky statistic, so it 
can be hard to get it right.  (It's easy to work with when writing 
theory papers, but less easy when writing empirical papers.  ;-))

> So far, following your and Martina?s suggestions, we have run several 
> models using directed shared partnership terms as well as a model with 
> esp(0). The latter model converged, but we find that although it 
> improves the GOF of the esp distribution, it considerably worsens the 
> fit for the out-degree distribution. Interestingly, our attempts with 
> dgwesp terms lead to similarly bad outcomes for the out-degree 
> distribution.
>
You might be able to make things work by combining esp(0) with a degree 
distribution term (gwodegree or some such).  You might also look at 
where things seem to be going wrong in the outdegree distribution to see 
if this suggests a possible missing covariate related to degree - in a 
complex system in which everything affects everything else, the thing 
that's missing isn't always in the place you expect.  :-)

> This is as far as we?ve gotten so far in our renewed attempts and it 
> will still probably take us a while to figure out the best solution, 
> but you?ve given us a lot of new ideas to try. Thanks for your response!
>

Glad this is helpful.  FWIW, you may at some point want to step back and 
think about whether one or another version of these models is adequate 
for your purposes, even if it gets a few things wrong. Models for 
complex systems rarely get everything right (hell, there are no models 
of liquid _water_ that recover all of its properties, and water is a lot 
simpler than a village!), so there is a point at which one has to make a 
judgment call about whether the model is good enough to be useful, even 
where it's not perfect.  Since your models are already doing well on 
many dimensions, I'm optimistic that you'll solve the puzzle, but you 
might be able to do a lot with what you already have.

Good luck!

-Carter
